_about: Explanations for the error codes the mistake spotter (and the rules) use. Written for Xenify; MIT. 'candidates' says how suggestions are found: words to try in the flagged spot, tested against the spotter.

apostrophe.title: Apostrophe
apostrophe.text: Apostrophes show who owns something (the team's results) or a missing letter (it's, don't). Plurals don't take one: apples, not apple's.

article_missing.title: Missing a, an or the
article_missing.text: Most single things in English need a, an or the in front: a dog, the station. Plural and uncountable words often don't (dogs, water).

article_wrong.title: Wrong a, an or the
article_wrong.text: Use an before a vowel sound (an hour, an apple) and a before a consonant sound (a university). The is for something specific; a is for any one.

comma_intro.title: Comma after an opening phrase
comma_intro.text: When a sentence starts with an opening word or clause (However, If you can, When we arrived), a comma marks where the main part begins.
examples: If you can come let me know.
If you can come, let me know.

comma_list_meaning.title: Commas in a list
comma_list_meaning.text: Missing commas can join list items into nonsense: "I love cooking my family and my pets" means something very different from "I love cooking, my family and my pets".
examples: She enjoys cooking her kids and her dog.
She enjoys cooking, her kids and her dog.

comma_splice.title: Two sentences joined by a comma
comma_splice.text: A comma alone can't join two complete sentences. Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a joining word (and, but, so).
examples: The meeting ran late, we missed the train.
The meeting ran late, so we missed the train.

comma_vocative.title: Comma around a name
comma_vocative.text: When you speak to someone by name, commas separate the name from the rest: "Thanks, John." Without it the meaning can change: "Let's eat Grandma."

comparative.title: More / most
comparative.text: Words that already compare (taller, easiest) don't need more or most: more taller → taller.

confused_words.title: Commonly confused words
confused_words.text: Some words look or sound alike but mean different things (affect/effect, accept/except, lose/loose). Check which meaning you want.

eggcorn.title: Misheard phrase
eggcorn.text: Some fixed phrases are often misheard and written wrongly: "for all intents and purposes", "nip it in the bud", "should have" (not "should of").
examples: Let's nip it in the butt.
Let's nip it in the bud.

fragment.title: Incomplete sentence
fragment.text: This reads as part of a sentence on its own (often starting with because, which or although). Join it to the sentence before, or add what's missing.
examples: We stopped. Because the server was down.
We stopped because the server was down.

homophone.title: Words that sound alike
homophone.text: Words like their/there/they're, your/you're and to/too/two sound the same but mean different things. A spell-checker can't tell them apart.

hyphen.title: Hyphen
hyphen.text: Two words working together as one description before a noun take a hyphen (a follow-up meeting, a well-known author). As a verb they stay apart (follow up with them).
examples: Let's schedule a follow up meeting.

its_its.title: Its or it's
its_its.text: It's means "it is" or "it has". Its means "belonging to it". If you can say "it is", write it's.

missing_word.title: A word is missing
missing_word.text: A small word seems to be missing here, often to, the, of, is or be. Read the sentence aloud and listen for the gap.
examples: We need to finish the draft.
missing_word.candidates: insert:to,the,a,of,is,are,be,for,that,it,in,on,with,and,was,have,will,to the,in the,of the,on the,at the,for the,to a,at

plural_form.title: Plural or uncountable
plural_form.text: Some words have unusual plurals (child → children) and some can't be counted at all (information, advice): "more information", not "informations".

preposition.title: Wrong small linking word
preposition.text: Words like in, on, at, for and to depend on the words around them: in 10 minutes (not on), listen to music (not listen music), depend on (not depend of).

pronoun_antecedent.title: Unclear or mismatched pronoun
pronoun_antecedent.text: A pronoun (he, she, it, they) should clearly point back to one thing and match it: "the department… it", not "the department… he".
examples: The fire department arrived, but he couldn't find the source.
The fire department arrived, but it couldn't find the source.

pronoun_case.title: I or me? He or him?
pronoun_case.text: Use I/he/she/we/they as the subject and me/him/her/us/them after verbs and words like for, with and between. Test by removing the other person.
examples: This is between you and I.
This is between you and me.

pronoun_verb_agreement.title: Verb doesn't match the pronoun
pronoun_verb_agreement.text: The verb has to match its subject: he goes, she doesn't, we were.

real_word_typo.title: Typo that's a real word
real_word_typo.text: A slip of the keys has made a different real word (pubic for public, manger for manager, form for from), so a spell-checker didn't notice.

sign_off.title: Greeting or sign-off
sign_off.text: Check the spelling and punctuation of the greeting and sign-off: Kind regards, Best wishes, Sincerely; and a comma after "Hi Sam,".

subject_verb_agreement.title: Verb doesn't match the subject
subject_verb_agreement.text: The verb matches the main word of the subject, not the nearest word: "The results of the test were", "Each of the students has".
examples: The results of the test was clear.
The results of the test were clear.

tense_shift.title: Change of tense
tense_shift.text: The sentence switches between past and present without a reason. Keep to one time frame: "She walked in and said hello."
examples: She walks in and said hello.
She walked in and said hello.

verb_form.title: Wrong verb form
verb_form.text: This verb form doesn't fit here: "I saw" or "I have seen" (not "I seen"), "has gone" (not "has went"), "to go" (not "to going").

verb_pattern.title: Verb pattern
verb_pattern.text: Some verbs need a particular next word or form: look forward to hearing, explain it to me, suggest that he go, let him go.
examples: I look forward to hear from you.
I look forward to hearing from you.

word_order.title: Word order
word_order.text: The words are in an unusual order. Inside a sentence, a question keeps normal order ("tell me where the office is"), and words like always go after am/is/are.
examples: Can you tell me where is the office?
Can you tell me where the office is?

garbled.title: Sentence may not make sense
garbled.text: Part of this sentence doesn't hold together: often words left over from an edit, a missing verb, words in a jumbled order or a sentence that stops too soon. Read it again and rewrite the part that's marked.
examples: We moved the meeting to Friday.
She sent the report to the.
She sent the report to the manager.
